transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28 15:00 PST
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Sarah Lee (CTO, Nimbus Health), Mike Alvarez (Platform Eng), Priya Singh (Security), Tom Reynolds (Product)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focusing on tracing, request logs, and error analysis flows. Customer wants to understand debug workflow for production incidents, what data is captured, and how to map trace IDs to request payloads and logs. Security questions around KMS, data retention, and RBAC surfaced. Agreed next steps to run a small POC and share security artifacts.

Topics:
- Console tracing UI and trace ID correlation
- Request logs and payload redaction
- Error analysis and root-cause workflows
- Integration with customer SIEM and KMS
- Pilot/POC next steps and success metrics

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone, thanks for joining, we can do 45 minutes, we'll go through the console flows and then leave time for q and a
[00:08] Sarah Lee: thanks maya, excited to see how you do tracing — we have a couple incidents last quarter where requests hung and we couldn't quickly figure out if it was kv cache or our prefixing
[00:16] Jordan Patel: yep, totally get it. I'll share my screen and walk through a live console session — focusing on trace ids, request logs, and the error analysis panel
[00:27] Mike Alvarez: cool. also want to know what we can hook into our splunk / datadog, and how payloads are stored, pinging priya for compliance side
[00:36] Priya Singh: yeah, i'm mostly concerned about pii in request logs and key management — do you support customer managed keys and can we restrict who sees full payloads
[00:45] Jordan Patel: short answer: yes to cmk/kms and rbac controls; i'll demo how redwood flags sensitive fields and how you can configure redaction. i'll start with the traces tab
[01:00] Jordan Patel (screen): so here's the traces view — you can see a list of recent traces with trace id, duration, model variant, and route. you can filter by status (success, errored, throttled) and by route name
[01:18] Jordan Patel: clicking into a trace shows the span timeline — you can see model latency, routing time, batch wait, and any fallback events. this helps quickly identify if the model step or the networking step caused the spike
[01:32] Tom Reynolds: is that batch wait the time your runtime spent waiting for enough tokens to batch?
[01:36] Jordan Patel: exactly, it's the continuous batching window. we show distribution so you can tune batch thresholds — and we also surface sample payloads if your policy allows it
[01:48] Sarah Lee: what's the retention for these traces? and can we export them to our SIEM?
[01:53] Jordan Patel: traces are retained configurable per plan — for dedicated/pv customers you can set longer retention. export — yes, we have an exports API and direct forwarders for datadog/splunk, also you can push to S3 for long term
[02:10] Priya Singh: and the payloads that show up in trace: are those raw? we need redaction for pph, health ids etc
[02:18] Jordan Patel: we have a policy engine — default redaction removes likely pii tokens, and you can define regex rules to scrub additional fields. when policy is on, traces show masked payload and you can request unmasked view which requires elevated RBAC audit
[02:36] Maya Chen: i'll add our security pack after the call, that has a short note on redaction and KMS flow
[02:43] Mike Alvarez: good. can you show an example of an errored request and how you would debug it
[02:48] Jordan Patel (screen): sure — clicking on an errored trace here, you can see the error summary at the top, stacks from the serving runtime if applicable, and the request log below. the error analysis view groups similar errors and suggests likely causes — e.g., model OOM, bad tokenization, or upstream 429 from an auth layer
[03:08] Jordan Patel: notice here the trace has a trace-id: trc_62b9f2 — you can paste that into the request logs or the API audit table and find the exact request payload and user metadata
[03:20] Sarah Lee: does the trace-id map back to our internal user id? we send a user_id field in metadata
[03:25] Jordan Patel: yes, the request logs index metadata fields (user_id, session_id, route) so correlation is straightforward. if you push logs to splunk, that mapping will carry over
[03:36] Tom Reynolds: how does the console handle noisy roots — like repeated transient 429s cause a lot of traces to show up
[03:42] Jordan Patel: we have noise filters and an anomaly detector; by default the error analysis groups by signature and surfaces the top contributing routes. you can mark a signature as noise or whitelist it for a time window
[03:55] Sarah Lee: what's logged for streaming responses? we do partial tokens and would like visibility into streaming failures mid-response
[04:03] Jordan Patel: streaming shows chunked events in the trace timeline — you'll see timestamps for each chunk and any mid-stream error will be logged with the last successful token position. the console also allows downloading the full event stream for playback
[04:18] Priya Singh: about encryption at rest, is the trace store encrypted with customer managed keys?
[04:24] Jordan Patel: for private/dedicated deployments we support customer-managed KMS; hosted customers can request CMK on higher tiers. I'll put the KMS flow diagram in the security pack
[04:34] Mike Alvarez: can Redwood redact full request bodies before storing them to the trace store? not just mask
[04:41] Jordan Patel: yes, you can choose mask vs drop. drop removes the field before it's persisted, mask keeps a deterministic token for correlation while hiding contents
[04:52] Maya Chen: quick note on login/console RBAC — you can limit who sees unmasked payloads and viewing requires an audited access event, that goes into the audit log
[05:02] Sarah Lee: good. any examples of root-cause from customer incidents?
[05:07] Jordan Patel: yeah, i'll show a recent example (obfuscated) — we had a case where latency spiked due to a fallback from quantized variant to full fp model because the KV cache hit rate dropped; trace showed long disk reads on the cache node and the error analysis suggested tuning cache TTL and warming prefixes
[05:25] Jordan Patel (screen): here you see the fallback event in the timeline and the console's suggestion to increase kv cache warmers — it links to the Optimize suggestions as well
[05:33] Tom Reynolds: so Optimize recommends quantization profiles and cache/binning settings?
[05:37] Jordan Patel: right — Optimize will analyze your workload and suggest quant profiles, batching thresholds, and cache TTLs. it can also simulate estimated cost impact of a change
[05:45] Sarah Lee: curious, can we run Optimize offline against a sample of our traffic to get suggestions before changing prod config?
[05:52] Jordan Patel: yes, we can ingest a traffic sample and run a dry-run. that's what we usually do in the POC
[05:58] Mike Alvarez: back to request logs — can we stream full logs with headers to our SIEM, or do you only allow redacted/metadata streams?
[06:06] Jordan Patel: by default we stream metadata+status; for full logs we require an outbound forwarder with an allowlist and customer opt-in, and for hosted we need a legal agreement around retention. for dedicated/private it's straightforward via forwarder or S3 sink
[06:20] Priya Singh: ok that's fine. what about alerting — can we get alerted on new error signatures at a configured threshold?
[06:28] Jordan Patel: yep, alerting hooks into the error analysis engine — you can configure thresholds per route, set severity, and route alerts to pagerduty/slack/webhook. we can show you the alert rule templates
[06:38] Sarah Lee: show me the request inspector — I want to see how a dev would debug a prod ticket
[06:44] Jordan Patel (screen): sure. the request inspector shows the request timeline, the full set of spans, the request metadata on the side, any policy flags (redaction, cmk used), and a quick link to the raw payload if allowed. you can also jump to the model performance tab which shows token-level costs and latency breakdown
[07:05] Mike Alvarez: token-level breakdown is huge — can we map token cost to feature flags? we have different routes with optional tools and sometimes tools inflate token counts
[07:13] Jordan Patel: yep you can tag requests with route-level metadata and feature flags; the console will slice token usage by tag so you can see per-feature cost. those tags can be passed in headers or set by your routing layer
[07:25] Tom Reynolds: one question on retention and compliance — if we need 1 year of audit logs, is that supported?
[07:31] Jordan Patel: for dedicated/private yes, full year retention is possible; hosted customers can export to S3 for long term or buy extended retention add-on
[07:40] Sarah Lee: can you show a drill-down of an error signature grouping?
[07:43] Jordan Patel (screen): hitting the error analysis page — here's a signature showing 182 occurrences in the last 7 days, top affected routes, sample traces, and a suggested remediation. you can create a ticket from the signature and assign it to an owner, or mark signatures as addressed
[08:02] Priya Singh: is the grouping deterministic? sometimes similar stack traces look different because of timestamps
[08:08] Jordan Patel: grouping uses normalized signatures — we strip timestamps and session-specific ids, and catalog by error class and span position. you can tweak similarity thresholds
[08:17] Sarah Lee: ok, we have a use case: during deployments we see a short window of elevated 500s — we want an automated rollback if a route error rate crosses x% and latency P95 > y. is that supported?
[08:29] Jordan Patel: yes, Redwood has rollout policies — you can define canary thresholds and automatic rollback policies. it integrates with the serving runtime so if error or latency crosses threshold it can shift traffic back to previous variant
[08:40] Mike Alvarez: that'll be useful. how do we map the rollout event to traces for postmortems?
[08:45] Jordan Patel: rollout events are annotated in traces and in the console timeline; every trace during a rollout gets a metadata field with rollout id so you can filter and compare pre/post
[08:54] Tom Reynolds: question from product: if we want to enable debug-level logging for a short window for just one user, can we do that without affecting others?
[08:59] Jordan Patel: yes, you can set targeted debug sessions by client id or user id; debug logs are kept for a short window and require elevated audit. there's also a 'just-in-time trace capture' that can be triggered from a request header for a single request
[09:14] Sarah Lee: that's awesome — avoids the usual noise of global debug flags
[09:19] Maya Chen: priya, any other security items?
[09:22] Priya Singh: can we see the retention policy and who in redwood can access raw logs? we need to present this to our auditor
[09:28] Maya Chen: yes, i'll include the access matrix in the security pack — it lists roles, access levels, and audit trail links
[09:35] Mike Alvarez: for the POC, can you provide a short checklist of what you need from our side? sample prompts, traffic distribution, and a few target success metrics?
[09:44] Jordan Patel: absolutely — we'll send a POC checklist: sample traffic (csv), expected qps, target latency p95, and any special redaction rules. we'll also create a test account and share keys
[09:55] Jordan Patel: quick demo of request log search — you can search by trace id, user_id, error code, model variant, or free text. results show snippet with context and link to trace
[10:08] Tom Reynolds: any limits on search? we have large volumes
[10:11] Jordan Patel: search is indexed; for high volume we recommend using exports to your data lake. we also expose a search API for programmatic queries with paging
[10:20] Sarah Lee: back to streaming — if a streaming request fails due to a mid-stream error, do you have automatic retries or resumable streams?
[10:27] Jordan Patel: we have client-visible retriable errors and support resumable streams for certain protocols; the console will show the retry attempts and final outcome
[10:36] Priya Singh: what's the SLA for hosted vs dedicated?
[10:39] Maya Chen: hosted has best-effort latency targets, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs. i'll share the SLA doc in the pack
[10:47] Mike Alvarez: anything else in the console for ops teams?
[10:49] Jordan Patel: there's a health dashboard, per-route metrics, token cost heatmaps, and the trace/search capabilities we showed. you can set synthetic monitors to run prompts periodically and alert on regressions
[11:01] Sarah Lee: let's discuss pilot scope — we'd like a week-long POC with a restricted set of routes, run Optimize on our sample traffic, and gather traces for two real incidents
[11:11] Maya Chen: sounds reasonable. target start?
[11:15] Sarah Lee: aiming for the week of 2025-02-10, pending internal approvals
[11:20] Jordan Patel: we'll prepare the POC checklist and provision a lower-latency test pool so you can replicate your peak qps
[11:26] Tom Reynolds: how will billing work for the POC? are there eval seats?
[11:30] Maya Chen: typically we provide credits for the POC; we'll outline the expected usage and proposed cap and you can approve
[11:36] Mike Alvarez: one last question — can we demo the API mapping to traces? i want to see the curl request and where it shows up in the console
[11:41] Jordan Patel (screen): sure — here's a sample curl with metadata headers: x-redwood-user, x-route, x-feature. hitting send... and you can see the trace appear with the same trace id. it populates the request inspector in near real-time
[11:55] Jordan Patel: sometimes the transcripts (auto) miss luh, like 'KV' becomes 'k v' — but click into the raw payload and you get the original fields
[12:04] Sarah Lee: haha yeah transcription for these calls is always quirky
[12:08] Maya Chen: ok we're at about 35 minutes in, maybe quick q and a and then wrap with next steps
[12:14] Priya Singh: one more compliance question: do you support dedicated on-prem installs?
[12:18] Maya Chen: yes, private on-prem is supported; that gives you full control of logs, retention, and KMS — Jordan can dig into the package in the technical deep-dive
[12:28] Sarah Lee: sounds good, please include estimated timeline and resource needs for on-prem eval
[12:33] Jordan Patel: will do.
[12:36] Tom Reynolds: thanks, this was helpful. we'll review and get you the traffic sample
[12:40] Maya Chen: thanks all — we'll send the security pack, POC checklist, and demo recording. next steps laid out in the calendar invite
[12:48] Sarah Lee: appreciate it, talk soon

End of transcript
